steps.observation: Work on this for 900 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Here’s a conceptual walkthrough of the Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al. 2017), broken into its core ideas and how they fit together:

1. Why Transformers?  
   Traditional sequence models (RNNs, LSTMs) process tokens one by one and have trouble capturing long-range dependencies in very long sequences. Transformers solve this by relying entirely on attention mechanisms, which let every token “look at” every other token in parallel.

2. Input Representation  
   – Token Embeddings: Each input token (word or subword) is mapped to a fixed-size vector via a learned embedding matrix.  
   – Positional Encodings: Because attention is permutation-invariant, we add a vector encoding each token’s position (e.g. via sinusoids or learned embeddings) so the model knows token order.

3. Self-Attention (“Scaled Dot-Product Attention”)  
   For a set of input vectors X = [x₁, x₂, …, xₙ]:  
   a) Project each xᵢ into three vectors: query qᵢ, key kᵢ, and value vᵢ, via learned linear projections.  
   b) Compute attention scores between every pair (i, j) as score(i, j) = (qᵢ · kⱼ) / √d_k, where d_k is key dimension (the √d_k “scaling” avoids overly large dot products).  
   c) Normalize scores for each i via softmax across j: aᵢⱼ = softmax_j(score(i, j)).  
   d) Compute the attended output for position i as oᵢ = Σⱼ aᵢⱼ · vⱼ.  
   In plain terms: each token “queries” all tokens’ keys, weighs their values, and sums them.

4. Multi-Head Attention  
   Instead of one set of Q/K/V projections, use H parallel “heads,” each with its own smaller projections.  
   – Each head attends in a different learned subspace, enabling the model to capture multiple relationships (e.g. syntactic vs. semantic).  
   – The H heads’ outputs are concatenated and linearly projected back to the model dimension.

5. Transformer Layer (Encoder Block)  
   Each encoder block has two sublayers, each wrapped with a residual connection and followed by layer normalization:  
   a) Multi-Head Self-Attention on the input.  
   b) Position-wise Feed-Forward Network (FFN): applies the same two-layer MLP to each position independently:  
      FFN(x) = max(0, xW₁ + b₁)W₂ + b₂.  
   The residual (“skip”) connections help gradient flow and let each sublayer learn only the difference from the identity.

6. Stacking Encoders  
   You stack N identical encoder blocks. The output of block i is fed into block i+1. Deeper stacks let the model build up more abstract representations.

7. Decoder (for Auto-Regressive / Seq2Seq Tasks)  
   The decoder is also a stack of blocks, but each block has three sublayers:  
   a) Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention: prevents each position from attending to future positions (enforces auto-regressive generation).  
   b) Multi-Head Cross-Attention over the encoder outputs: queries come from the decoder’s previous sublayer, keys/values from the encoder’s final outputs.  
   c) Position-wise FFN.  
   Again, residual connections + layer norms wrap each sublayer.

8. Generating Output  
   – After the decoder’s final layer, apply a linear projection plus softmax to turn each position’s vector into a probability distribution over the vocabulary.  
   – During training, we use teacher forcing (feeding the ground-truth previous token). During inference, we sample or beam-search one token at a time, re-feeding it into the decoder.

9. Training Objective  
   Typically cross-entropy loss comparing the predicted distribution at each position to the actual next token. Optimization is via Adam (or variants) with learning-rate warmup and decay.

10. Key Takeaways  
   – Attention is the heart: every output token can flexibly combine information from the entire input (or past outputs).  
   – No recurrence or convolution—full parallelism over sequence length.  
   – Positional encodings inject order information.  
   – Multi-head attention lets the model capture diverse patterns and relations.  
   – Residual connections + layer norm make very deep stacks trainable.

In effect, a Transformer magic trick is: “Represent each token, ask it to attend to all tokens (including itself), enrich its representation, then pass it through a small feed-forward network. Repeat.” By stacking many such blocks, you get powerful contextualized embeddings that can be decoded back into sequences or classifications.
